October 28 13:30 UTC: Continued monitoring

Sophos is monitoring third-party reporting of PHP2Shell exploitation but has not confirmed the claims. As of this update, there has been no evidence of exploitation in Sophos customer telemetry. 

Due to the widespread use of PHP, a successful exploit would be a likely addition to toolkits for threat actors conducting targeted attacks. Upgrading to PHP versions that address the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) remains the best defense. 

The Sophos blog post "The breachpocalypse is here" discusses the implications of PHP2Shell and other compromises and vulnerabilities observed in October.

October 23 15:35 UTC: Note about additional PHP vulnerability and new PHP2Shell countermeasures

On October 23, PHP released an informational advisory disclosing another remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-115560). The advisory states that the issue requires “an unusual combination of configuration and application code” and that mitigations published for PHP2Shell vulnerability CVE-2026-109619 also address this threat. Sophos will continue to monitor the vulnerability and will release updated information and additional countermeasures as appropriate. 

SophosLabs has also released additional PHP2Shell countermeasures, specifically Sophos Firewall and Endpoint IPS signatures 213184, 213185, 213187, 213188, and 213189.

October 22 21:21 UTC: Correction and new insights, countermeasures, and indicators

The previous update (October 22 16:18 UTC) reported that Sophos observed successful exploitation of PHP2Shell in customer environments. Upon further analysis, we are correcting that assessment as Sophos customer telemetry shows scanning and a small number of failed exploitation attempts. As of this update, there is no evidence of a successful compromise due to these vulnerabilities.

The payload, a likely Mirai botnet variant known as Potassium, was not delivered since the exploitation attempt was unsuccessful due to being blocked by Sophos countermeasures. However, analysis of the sample revealed that is an updated and significantly expanded version of the Mirai-derived botnet variant identified in early 2026. The sample displays downloader and network disruption functionality. It resolves a hard-coded, encrypted C2 address; establishes a TCP connection to 134[.]199[.]154[.]64; and sends an HTTP request. It checks for an HTTP 200 response status and verifies that the resulting payload begins with the ELF magic bytes 7F 45 4C 46, indicating that it expects to retrieve a Linux ELF follow-on payload. A resolver function supports IPv4 addresses and hostname resolution, with additional fallback resolution logic that includes hard-coded public DNS servers such as 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1, and 1.0.0.1. As with Mirai malware historically, this sample can execute DDoS attacks.

Sophos analysis of the vulnerabilities suggests that developing a successful exploit is not straightforward. The Sophos Adversary Group has been attempting to produce a successful exploit, which is proving challenging even with AI support. The lack of successful exploits in the wild suggests threat actors are also struggling. Security researchers have claimed they have developed successful exploits, but it is possible these only work in lab scenarios rather than real-world environments. Successful exploitation may also require certain dependencies or configurations. Despite the low level of activity, the vulnerabilities remain serious. Given time, threat actors may develop successful exploits. Urgent patching remains the primary recommendation.

The following new Sophos countermeasures relate to this threat:

  • Sophos Firewall IPS signatures 67359, 67360, 67375, 2313184, 2313185, 2313187 and 2313188
  • Sophos Endpoint IPS signatures 2313184, 2313185, 2313187, 2313188 and 2313189

These join existing Sophos endpoint XDR, Taegis XDR, Windows Behavioral Protection, and Linux Runtime Detection rules.

Proof-of-concept exploit code is publicly available, and Sophos threat hunters have identified multiple exploit attempts consistent with PHP2Shell activity and one successful exploitation. While Sophos analysis have concluded that exploitation of these vulnerabilities is viable, successful follow-on remote code execution depends on deployment architecture, PHP version, and configuration. As of this update, Sophos analysts have not observed evidence linking the activity to ransomware deployment, data theft, or supply chain compromise.

The following behaviors and changes may indicate exploitation of these vulnerabilities:

  • Network sessions that last longer than usual (Applications running on the PHP service should have a standard pattern of network connections.)
  • Unusual process names (including misspellings of legitimate names), or seemingly legitimate processes in unexpected locations
  • Unusual and low-volume inbound traffic from low-reputation infrastructure

October 21 14:28 UTC: Revised version of the original advisory (published at approximately 12:55 UTC) following PHP’s release of updates and additional details

Overview

On October 20, 2026, PHP announced an upcoming security release to address two critical (CVSS score of 9.2) vulnerabilities. Third-party sources identified the vulnerabilities as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. According to reports, the issues impact multiple PHP versions and allow for remote code execution. 

On October 21, PHP released updated versions to address these issues and stated that “all PHP installations serving web requests” are at risk. A user on the X platform claims to have created a working proof-of-concept exploit. As of this publication, active exploitation has not been reported in the wild.

Recommended actions

Counter Threat Unit™ researchers recommend that customers identify potentially vulnerable systems and upgrade as appropriate. In the interim, organizations should consider taking internet-facing PHP-powered systems offline if feasible or putting them behind network-layer authentication (e.g., ZTNA). Additionally, network defenders should evaluate the potential for exploitation in their environment and monitor for suspicious activity. The PHP advisory lists mitigations for organizations who cannot immediately upgrade but notes that updating is the only complete solution. 

Sophos countermeasures

SophosLabs continues to monitor the threat landscape for activity related to these vulnerabilities and will deliver detections and protections as available. An internal investigation is also underway to determine if Sophos products or services are affected.

item.title: Web App Owners – You’re on Notice. Your Low-Hanging Fruit Just Got Lower
item.description:
This article is part of an ongoing series from Sophos frontline security operations specialists, sharing the expertise they use to strengthen our industry-leading Managed Detection and Response (MDR) service and defend customers against evolving AI-era threats.

The cybersecurity industry has spent years preparing for attackers who automate reconnaissance, vulnerability scanning, and credential attacks. What is changing now is the degree to which automation can connect those individual activities into a sustained intrusion workflow.

Recent Sophos Incident Response investigations illustrate this shift. The incidents affected unrelated organizations in different industries and relied on different initial-access paths. Yet the operational patterns were strikingly similar: rapid reconnaissance, repetitive testing, credential discovery, privilege-escalation attempts, lateral movement, data-access validation, persistence, and systematic cleanup.

The evidence points to the use of systems consistent with machine-speed tooling likely associated with the use of an AI agent or orchestration framework. There were no user-agent strings, or specific signatures that called out AI-based tools.  However, the speed, breadth, repetition, and adaptability observed in the incidents demonstrate why distinguishing between a skilled operator, scripted automation, and an AI-assisted attacker is becoming increasingly difficult.

More importantly, defenders may soon find that the distinction matters less than the outcome.

From Isolated Techniques to an End-to-End Attack Process

Traditional security analysis often examines attacker behavior as a collection of individual techniques:

  • SQL injection
  • Web-shell deployment
  • Credential discovery
  • Privilege escalation
  • Remote service access
  • Lateral movement
  • Data collection
  • Log or artifact deletion

Viewed individually, none of these techniques are new. What stood out in these incidents was how quickly they were connected into coherent attack sequences.  The environments and access paths were different. The attacker behavior was not.  Like any attacker, reconnaissance was performed to identify potential weaknesses in systems.  Then, the attacker exploits those weaknesses and moves on to further their objectives.

Incident Pattern One: Database Access Becomes Enterprise Access

In one case, the threat actor turned access to SQL infrastructure into a broader enterprise intrusion.

The observed activity included:

1. Web Application enumeration

The threat actor was observed probing multiple web applications in parallel and attempted to enumerate directories with varying degrees of success.  This is typical of blind application scanning when the adversary does not know sub-directories or the layout of the application.

2. SQL and web application probing

Internet-facing systems received repeated SQL injection techniques. This ultimately resulted in the successful enabling of xp_cmdshell.  Also notable was that the web application enumeration observed leading up to the successful xp_cmdshell activity stopped.

3. Command execution through database services

Subsequent telemetry showed SQL Server processes launching command shells and PowerShell consistent with the use of xp_cmdshell. The attacker used common discovery commands, tested remote command execution, enumerated linked servers, and assessed whether SQL functionality could be used to reach additional hosts.

4. Privilege-escalation attempts

The attacker staged or executed tooling consistent with token impersonation and service-account privilege escalation. In some instances, output files were used to check whether commands had reached a higher-privileged security context. Several privilege-escalation events were observed from the available telemetry.

5. Credential discovery and collection

Activity included searches through configuration and script files, attempts to save sensitive Windows registry hives, detection of LSASS-related credential access, and inspection of stored credentials and application secrets. Some credential-harvesting activity was blocked by endpoint controls.

6. Lateral movement at scale

The attacker queried administrative shares, tested remote SQL access, used WMI and scheduled tasks, and created remote tasks configured to execute under privileged accounts. Multiple servers were tested in quick succession.

Once xp_cmdshell was enabled, it would execute under the database server account.  In this instance, like many others, this was a service account on the server with high privileges.  This sequence demonstrates how a service account or database execution context can become a launch point for enterprise-wide discovery. This is not new. 

This is typical of activity observed with human operators, but the speed of pivoting and follow-on telemetry pointed to automated actions.  A database server may appear to be a specialized application asset, but its network reach, service credentials, linked servers, administrative tools, and access to other systems can make it a powerful pivot point for attackers.  From the start of web application enumeration to gaining xp_cmdshell was 1 hour 45 minutes.  The time on target until hosts were isolated was 30 minutes.

Incident Pattern Two: A File Upload Becomes a Cloud and Data Access Path

The second investigation followed a different route but produced a similarly broad attack sequence.

Application activity indicated abuse of account-management or password-reset functionality, followed by access to customer-related application data and use of an upload endpoint that accepted server-executable files. The attacker then deployed multiple web shells across several web servers.

Once established, the attacker moved quickly:

1. Web Application enumeration

Like the earlier incident, the threat actor was observed probing multiple web applications in parallel.  However, of note, was that once the webshell was uploaded on the first, the scanning of other applications persisted.  Ultimately 2 web applications were exploited, however this was the same code-base as it was a dev and prod version of the same site.

2. Web-shell execution

IIS worker processes launched command shells under application-pool identities. The attacker issued identity checks, listed websites and application pools, enumerated users and administrators, and explored accessible directories.

3. Configuration and secret harvesting

The attacker read multiple web.config files and searched for private keys, certificates, deployment profiles, environment files, unattended-installation files, and stored Windows credentials. Not only did this focus on web.config files in the application directories, but it also searched across multiple drives which found Service Principal Names (SPN’s) for applications no longer in use.  Those collected SPN’s were later seen attempting logons from suspicious IP addresses.

4. Cloud credential discovery

Commands queried the instance metadata service and attempted to recover temporary cloud credentials. The attacker also compiled and ran a dedicated metadata-access utility on multiple compromised systems.

5. Production database access

Credentials recovered or available in the environment were used to connect to production and staging SQL systems. The attacker enumerated databases and tables and submitted queries. Our investigation noted queries were run, but to obtain meta data about the database and were not observed doing bulk data extraction.  

6. Internal service access

The attacker found credentials for an internal file-transfer service, enumerated directories, tested write access, requested several files, and probed the host for additional reachable services.   This was associated with internal FTP services and leveraged obtained credentials found stored in plain text files across the systems.  Attempts were made to access RDP on multiple remote systems but were unsuccessful.

7. Privilege escalation and cleanup

The attacker retrieved privilege-escalation tooling, staged custom loaders, compiled utilities using software already present in the environment, and later issued commands to delete temporary directories and shell copies.

In this incident, it took the threat actor just over 3 hours to identify and exploit a file upload vulnerability.  Once webshells were successfully uploaded and executed, the threat actor remained on target for 1 hour 45 minutes before the affected systems were isolated.  

The investigation confirmed web-shell execution, credential and configuration discovery, database-access activity, internal service access, and cleanup attempts.  What was also discovered was that a critical business application was running on the same systems as a much older and less critical site.  While not directly targeted, the critical application became part of the blast radius when the older and vulnerable site was exploited.  

Why This Resembles AI-Assisted Intrusion Activity

In both incidents cited above, threat actors achieved initial access in under 3 hours. A recent Gambit Security report [1] documented a campaign in which open-source AI harnesses performed vulnerability discovery and exploitation against hundreds of online retailers. Between September 10 and September 15, 2026, the researchers identified 105 attack projects and at least 27 organizations compromised to varying degrees. The reported campaign used three components: Strix for vulnerability research, Cairn for autonomous exploitation, and Hermes for orchestration and operator guidance.

According to the report, the tools could receive broad objectives such as obtaining a shell or administrator access and then continue probing for hours with limited human intervention. The campaign reportedly cost an average of approximately $25.46 per completed scan, with attacks against some targets costing only a few dollars.

In the two incidents referenced above, there was no signature that identified this as being performed by an AI-enabled threat actor.  To learn more about what we were dealing with, we needed to go to the sources.  Using OSINT, we learned that the source systems involved in these incidents were running:

  • Cairn
  • CyberStrike AI
  • Cupcake-C2

Cairn is an open-source AI-driven state-space search engine designed to solve complex goal-oriented problems by exploring possible paths from a known starting state to a desired outcome. The project was initially validated in the domain of autonomous penetration testing but is intended as a more general-purpose problem-solving framework.

CyberStrikeAI is an open-source AI-powered autonomous security testing framework designed to assist with penetration testing and complex security assessments. The project combines large language models (LLMs) with automated decision-making workflows to explore, analyze, and pursue security testing objectives with minimal human intervention.

CupcakeC2 is an open-source Command-and-Control (C2) framework designed for red team operations, adversary emulation, and security research. According to the project's GitHub repository, it features a Rust-based agent, a Go-based server with support for cross-platform operation and integration with the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

These tools, plus the use of web vulnerability scanners and simple http servers that hosted post-exploitation tools such as webshells, and privilege escalation binaries, provide an attacker with the opportunity to exploit internet-facing web vulnerabilities with minimal human interaction that would have been time-consuming to take advantage of years earlier.  The two incident-response cases described an environment in which AI-enabled attackers could be highly effective:

  • Internet-facing applications exposed multiple pathways for exploration.
  • Application and service accounts had access beyond a single workload.
  • Configuration files contained or provided access to reusable credentials.
  • Web servers could initiate connections to internal databases and services.
  • Native compilers, PowerShell, command shells, and administrative utilities were available.
  • Similar actions could be repeated rapidly across many systems.
  • Cleanup commands were issued after tools and persistence mechanisms were tested.

This underpins the importance of everyday cybersecurity hygiene.  An autonomous attack agent does not require a previously unknown exploit if the environment exposes enough weakly connected controls. The agent can repeatedly test ordinary weaknesses until several of them form a viable attack path.

The Real Advantage Is Persistence, Not Novelty

AI-enabled intrusion activity should not be understood simply as “faster vulnerability scanning.” Its greater advantage is operational persistence.

A human operator becomes fatigued. A human operator may abandon a difficult target after several failed attempts. An autonomous system can enumerate another directory, decode another configuration file, try the next service, adjust a query, create a small utility, test a different credential, and continue for hours while the human operator rests up or enjoys a cup of tea.

Defending Against the Workflow, Not Just the Tool

Organizations will not reliably identify AI-enabled attacks by searching for an “AI malware” signature. The underlying techniques still appear as familiar operating-system, application, database, and cloud activity. Defenders should instead detect the sequence.

1. Treat application behavior as security telemetry

Authentication, password-reset, file-upload, administrative, and data-export endpoints should produce high-quality audit logs. Repeated requests across account-management and upload functions should be correlated as a single behavioral chain rather than reviewed as unrelated web events.

2. Prevent uploaded files from becoming executable content

User-controlled uploads should be stored outside executable web roots, renamed by the application, validated by content rather than extension, and served from isolated storage where server-side execution is impossible.

3. Remove secrets from configuration files

Application configuration should not expose long-lived database passwords, cloud credentials, private keys, or service-account secrets. Use managed identities or centralized secret stores, apply short credential lifetimes, and rotate any secret exposed to a compromised application host.

4. Restrict application-server egress

Web and database servers should communicate only with explicitly required destinations and ports. A compromised IIS worker process should not be able to query cloud metadata, download arbitrary executables, scan internal networks, or access unrelated administrative services.

5. Monitor abnormal parent-child process relationships

High-value detections include:

  • Web-server processes launching command shells
  • Database services spawning PowerShell
  • Service accounts running reconnaissance utilities
  • Compilers producing executables in temporary directories
  • PowerShell loading assemblies from decoded byte arrays
  • Application processes accessing instance metadata services
  • Remote scheduled tasks created by database or web-service accounts

6. Detect behavioral sequences

A single whoami command may be inconclusive. A sequence of whoami, network enumeration, configuration-file access, credential search, internal connection attempts, tool staging, and deletion is far more meaningful.

7. Design containment for machine-speed attacks

Containment procedures must account for an attacker that can execute hundreds of actions while a human analyst is still assembling the timeline. High-confidence web-shell or service-account compromise may require automated isolation, credential revocation, cloud-token invalidation, and temporary egress restrictions.

The Defender’s Time Horizon Has Changed

The lesson is that the attack paths that might have once been considered difficult to access and exploit by human operators are now well suited to autonomous execution.  An attacker no longer needs to manually investigate every file, endpoint, account, database, and host. AI-enabled tooling can preserve context, adapt commands, interpret output, generate small utilities, and continue testing until it finds the next workable step. These findings suggest this is no longer hypothetical.  Autonomous harnesses have been observed conducting substantial portions of real-world intrusion chains at low marginal cost.

Defensive programs built around human attacker speed will struggle in this environment. The answer is not simply more alerts. It is tighter application design, stronger identity boundaries, better segmentation, correlated behavioral detection, and containment capable of operating at comparable speed.  

The individual techniques may be familiar. The scale, endurance, and economics are not.  Owners of public-facing web applications should take immediate action to review their application architecture, reduce their attack surface, perform a business impact assessment of their applications, conduct Web Application Security Assessments and reduce the risk of a compromise before it’s too late.

Commands queried the instance metadata service and attempted to recover temporary cloud credentials. The attacker also compiled and ran a dedicated metadata-access utility on multiple compromised systems.

5. Production database access

Credentials recovered or available in the environment were used to connect to production and staging SQL systems. The attacker enumerated databases and tables and submitted queries. Our investigation noted queries were run, but to obtain meta data about the database and were not observed doing bulk data extraction.  

6. Internal service access

The attacker found credentials for an internal file-transfer service, enumerated directories, tested write access, requested several files, and probed the host for additional reachable services.   This was associated with internal FTP services and leveraged obtained credentials found stored in plain text files across the systems.  Attempts were made to access RDP on multiple remote systems but were unsuccessful.

7. Privilege escalation and cleanup

The attacker retrieved privilege-escalation tooling, staged custom loaders, compiled utilities using software already present in the environment, and later issued commands to delete temporary directories and shell copies.

In this incident, it took the threat actor just over 3 hours to identify and exploit a file upload vulnerability.  Once webshells were successfully uploaded and executed, the threat actor remained on target for 1 hour 45 minutes before the affected systems were isolated.  

The investigation confirmed web-shell execution, credential and configuration discovery, database-access activity, internal service access, and cleanup attempts.  What was also discovered was that a critical business application was running on the same systems as a much older and less critical site.  While not directly targeted, the critical application became part of the blast radius when the older and vulnerable site was exploited.  

Why This Resembles AI-Assisted Intrusion Activity

In both incidents cited above, threat actors achieved initial access in under 3 hours. A recent Gambit Security report [1] documented a campaign in which open-source AI harnesses performed vulnerability discovery and exploitation against hundreds of online retailers. Between September 10 and September 15, 2026, the researchers identified 105 attack projects and at least 27 organizations compromised to varying degrees. The reported campaign used three components: Strix for vulnerability research, Cairn for autonomous exploitation, and Hermes for orchestration and operator guidance.

According to the report, the tools could receive broad objectives such as obtaining a shell or administrator access and then continue probing for hours with limited human intervention. The campaign reportedly cost an average of approximately $25.46 per completed scan, with attacks against some targets costing only a few dollars.

In the two incidents referenced above, there was no signature that identified this as being performed by an AI-enabled threat actor.  To learn more about what we were dealing with, we needed to go to the sources.  Using OSINT, we learned that the source systems involved in these incidents were running:

  • Cairn
  • CyberStrike AI
  • Cupcake-C2

Cairn is an open-source AI-driven state-space search engine designed to solve complex goal-oriented problems by exploring possible paths from a known starting state to a desired outcome. The project was initially validated in the domain of autonomous penetration testing but is intended as a more general-purpose problem-solving framework.

CyberStrikeAI is an open-source AI-powered autonomous security testing framework designed to assist with penetration testing and complex security assessments. The project combines large language models (LLMs) with automated decision-making workflows to explore, analyze, and pursue security testing objectives with minimal human intervention.

CupcakeC2 is an open-source Command-and-Control (C2) framework designed for red team operations, adversary emulation, and security research. According to the project's GitHub repository, it features a Rust-based agent, a Go-based server with support for cross-platform operation and integration with the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

These tools, plus the use of web vulnerability scanners and simple http servers that hosted post-exploitation tools such as webshells, and privilege escalation binaries, provide an attacker with the opportunity to exploit internet-facing web vulnerabilities with minimal human interaction that would have been time-consuming to take advantage of years earlier.  The two incident-response cases described an environment in which AI-enabled attackers could be highly effective:

  • Internet-facing applications exposed multiple pathways for exploration.
  • Application and service accounts had access beyond a single workload.
  • Configuration files contained or provided access to reusable credentials.
  • Web servers could initiate connections to internal databases and services.
  • Native compilers, PowerShell, command shells, and administrative utilities were available.
  • Similar actions could be repeated rapidly across many systems.
  • Cleanup commands were issued after tools and persistence mechanisms were tested.

This underpins the importance of everyday cybersecurity hygiene.  An autonomous attack agent does not require a previously unknown exploit if the environment exposes enough weakly connected controls. The agent can repeatedly test ordinary weaknesses until several of them form a viable attack path.

The Real Advantage Is Persistence, Not Novelty

AI-enabled intrusion activity should not be understood simply as “faster vulnerability scanning.” Its greater advantage is operational persistence.

A human operator becomes fatigued. A human operator may abandon a difficult target after several failed attempts. An autonomous system can enumerate another directory, decode another configuration file, try the next service, adjust a query, create a small utility, test a different credential, and continue for hours while the human operator rests up or enjoys a cup of tea.

Defending Against the Workflow, Not Just the Tool

Organizations will not reliably identify AI-enabled attacks by searching for an “AI malware” signature. The underlying techniques still appear as familiar operating-system, application, database, and cloud activity. Defenders should instead detect the sequence.

1. Treat application behavior as security telemetry

Authentication, password-reset, file-upload, administrative, and data-export endpoints should produce high-quality audit logs. Repeated requests across account-management and upload functions should be correlated as a single behavioral chain rather than reviewed as unrelated web events.

2. Prevent uploaded files from becoming executable content

User-controlled uploads should be stored outside executable web roots, renamed by the application, validated by content rather than extension, and served from isolated storage where server-side execution is impossible.

3. Remove secrets from configuration files

Application configuration should not expose long-lived database passwords, cloud credentials, private keys, or service-account secrets. Use managed identities or centralized secret stores, apply short credential lifetimes, and rotate any secret exposed to a compromised application host.

4. Restrict application-server egress

Web and database servers should communicate only with explicitly required destinations and ports. A compromised IIS worker process should not be able to query cloud metadata, download arbitrary executables, scan internal networks, or access unrelated administrative services.

5. Monitor abnormal parent-child process relationships

High-value detections include:

  • Web-server processes launching command shells
  • Database services spawning PowerShell
  • Service accounts running reconnaissance utilities
  • Compilers producing executables in temporary directories
  • PowerShell loading assemblies from decoded byte arrays
  • Application processes accessing instance metadata services
  • Remote scheduled tasks created by database or web-service accounts

6. Detect behavioral sequences

A single whoami command may be inconclusive. A sequence of whoami, network enumeration, configuration-file access, credential search, internal connection attempts, tool staging, and deletion is far more meaningful.

7. Design containment for machine-speed attacks

Containment procedures must account for an attacker that can execute hundreds of actions while a human analyst is still assembling the timeline. High-confidence web-shell or service-account compromise may require automated isolation, credential revocation, cloud-token invalidation, and temporary egress restrictions.

The Defender’s Time Horizon Has Changed

The lesson is that the attack paths that might have once been considered difficult to access and exploit by human operators are now well suited to autonomous execution.  An attacker no longer needs to manually investigate every file, endpoint, account, database, and host. AI-enabled tooling can preserve context, adapt commands, interpret output, generate small utilities, and continue testing until it finds the next workable step. These findings suggest this is no longer hypothetical.  Autonomous harnesses have been observed conducting substantial portions of real-world intrusion chains at low marginal cost.

Defensive programs built around human attacker speed will struggle in this environment. The answer is not simply more alerts. It is tighter application design, stronger identity boundaries, better segmentation, correlated behavioral detection, and containment capable of operating at comparable speed.  

The individual techniques may be familiar. The scale, endurance, and economics are not.  Owners of public-facing web applications should take immediate action to review their application architecture, reduce their attack surface, perform a business impact assessment of their applications, conduct Web Application Security Assessments and reduce the risk of a compromise before it’s too late.

item.title: Is “SIEM-less” really what it sounds like?
item.description:
A SIEM is a multipurpose tool. It brings together cyber and physical security use cases; drives threat detection, investigation, and response (TDIR); serves as a system of record for governance, regulatory, and compliance needs; and supports observability use cases tied to resilience and service degradation. The list goes on.

In short, a SIEM is what an organization wants it to be. Therein lies both its strengths and its weaknesses.

The SIEM paradox

A SIEM can be a powerful “single pane of glass.” But that strength comes with two persistent challenges: operational complexity and data-ingestion costs.

Does more data mean better outcomes?

SIEMs store vast amounts of data. As the attack surface expands, organizations keep adding sources. Yet not all data serve the same purpose:

  • Detection and prevention require one set of data.
  • Investigations need contextual data to explain what happened.
  • Audit and compliance depend on evidence retained for reporting and review.

Because teams cannot always predict what they will need in the future, the default is often to ingest everything “just in case.” That is where the problems begin to compound.

Complexity comes first

The first symptoms are operational. Teams must determine which data is useful, why it matters, and how it should be applied in a particular context. Then they must be able to find it, search it, report on it, and turn it into something actionable when the moment comes.

Then comes the bill

Once the operational burden is established, the financial impact follows, often in the form of escalating ingestion costs.

How the SIEM became the center of the SOC

Over time, the SIEM also subsumed technologies that had once stood alone such as threat intelligence platforms, user and entity behavior analytics (UEBA), and security orchestration, automation, and response (SOAR). Each addition promised better context, stronger detection, or a tighter response loop.

Very quickly, the SOC was built around the SIEM, and the SIEM became fossilized in SOC processes and vendors took advantage of the “lock in”. Enter the era of SIEM deconstruction, and with it, the promised benefits of going “SIEM-less.”

Deconstructing the SIEM

Ingestion-based pricing crushing you with costs? Not to worry. Add a smart ingestion pipeline that filters out what you do not need before you store it. While you are at it, run detections in the pipeline. Et voilà, you have reduced storage costs and gained detections along the way.

Need to search the data in place? Add another component that can search across sources by translating queries for each one. Need to triage and investigate all those “detections” to determine what is worth chasing? Add an agentic SOC that promises to automate it all away.

Pretty soon, the collection starts to sound a lot like security information and event management, a SIEM. The difference is that the costs are now spread across individual components. It starts to look like unbundled pricing, where savings in one place create compute costs, or compromises, somewhere else.

The real cost driver: Compute

It is important not to confuse data-ingestion costs with storage costs. Processing data for upstream use cases requires compute; deciding how much data to retain, and for how long, requires storage. Even at today’s storage prices, compute costs dwarf storage costs.

Compute is the real cost driver. It is consumed when data is filtered, indexed for faster retrieval, queried, or used to generate reports. More compute is required when data must be rehydrated, moved from cold storage back into hot storage for analysis. Any or all of these costs can ultimately be passed on to the buyer.

A deconstructed architecture does not eliminate the underlying tasks or the ‘jobs to be done’. They still exist; they are simply carried out differently than they would be in a traditional SIEM.

Is SIEM-less a bad idea?

Actually, no. It can be the right call for an organization with the expertise and resources to build and maintain such a system. These new approaches are reshaping the economics and forcing traditional vendors to rethink their go-to-market strategies.

But a SIEM is ultimately a set of capabilities assembled into an architecture. Over time, every vendor offering one piece of the SIEM-less story will add adjacent capabilities until the resulting offering starts to look like, you guessed it, a SIEM.

Organizations that need a SIEM, therefore, face a practical choice: take the DIY route or invest in a fully integrated system with the right economics. At the end of the day, that choice matters.

So, where does XDR fit into all of this? More on that in my next blog.

item.title: The breachpocalypse is here
item.description:
Seven incidents in seven days

Last week I sent our leadership team a list. In seven days, Sophos' internal SecOps team responded to seven incidents: abuse of one of our products via a trial account, the ConnectWise Cloud Backup compromise, PHP2Shell, the eMudhra weak SubCAs, the second supply-chain compromise of LiteLLM this year, critical Node.js vulnerabilities and a GitLab RCE. A year ago, that would have been a quarter's worth.

We avoided major impact, but only through a concerted effort and some very long hours. Admittedly this is a sample size of one, but from my position protecting a leading cybersecurity vendor, the trend seems pretty clear.

"So where is the impact?"

The counter-argument is that the damage isn't showing up. PHP2Shell has not, so far, become the mass-exploitation event many of us braced for. There has been no "Challenger disaster", Simon Willison's phrase for the headline event that ends our normalisation of deviance. Tal Be'ery found that material-incident filings to the SEC rose only mildly in Q2 and Q3 2026, while high and critical CVEs rose several-fold.

I take that seriously. But we have always been bad at measuring a rising tide until well after it has risen. In 2012, the late Ross Anderson and colleagues counted over 100 sources of cybercrime data, all "insufficient and fragmented." Microsoft researchers showed that one survey respondent claiming $50,000 in losses could produce a $10 billion national estimate. Only in 2019 could Anderson's team confirm what they had guessed in 2012: cybercrime was about half of all crime. Dan Geer noted that 70–80% of breaches are found by third parties, so many victims may never know.

Public health offers a close parallel. Between 1999 and 2017, the US drug overdose death rate more than tripled, reaching 70,237 deaths a year. The toll built up from thousands of individual deaths, each logged by a local coroner, with no single disaster to mark it. The US did not declare a public health emergency until October 2017, and even then the count was off: opioid deaths were undercounted by 20–35% because death certificates often omitted the drug. A plane crash is counted by nightfall. A rising tide of small incidents is counted years later, and badly. Cyber's recent damage has come the same way: a growing stream of smaller incidents, with no mega-incident to count.

There's also some hard-earned mitigation to account for. Vendors, maintainers and security teams have patched at a pace I have never seen; Mozilla alone fixed 271 Firefox bugs from one AI-assisted effort and Sophos' own engineering team have been flat-out on the bugs emerging from our own Glasswing and Daybreak participation. But that doesn't hold below the security poverty line: the organisations lacking the money, expertise, and capability to protect themselves. They don't file 8-Ks or hold IR retainers. The most exposed cohort is also the one we measure worst.

The signals we do have

Operational signals arrive well before formal measurement. On 19 October, former NSA cybersecurity director Rob Joyce wrote that "IR firms are saturated & turning away work." That matches what we see: our own IR function has never been busier and is forecasting an industry-wide capacity crunch.

Similarly, Google Threat Intelligence reported 141 vulnerabilities exploited from January to August 2026, against 127 in all of 2025, and Anthropic research shows that the autonomous attack pattern it documented in 2025 "has now proliferated across every class of actors we investigated."

There is also a reporting asymmetry. Finding vulnerabilities is loud: researchers and AI labs publish counts, such as Project Glasswing's 10,000+ high or critical findings in a month. Incidents are quiet. In Bitdefender's 2026 survey, 55% of professionals who had suffered a breach were told to keep it confidential when they believed it should be reported. People brag about finding bugs. Nobody brags about being breached.

The frontier is jagged for attackers too

AI capability is a jagged frontier: strong at some tasks, surprisingly weak at neighbouring ones. Defenders haven't fully scaled their use of it, and neither have adversaries. RUSI's Will Lyne and Jamie MacColl argue that AI "is not (yet) fundamentally reinventing cybercrime", because criminals change business models only when profits force them to. Be'ery makes a similar case: monetisation and laundering, not vulnerabilities, are the bottleneck.

Both are plausible. A less comfortable view is that the binding constraint is the number of capable criminals, and AI is precisely a way to scale people.

Sophos X-Ops research shows we are at the early-adopter stage. When monitoring underground forums we found a clear knowledge gap: criminals buying brokered API keys and asking each other for basic setup help. A year of our MDR casework found that where attackers used AI, it was "as an assistant with a human in control." Observed adoption trails available capability. That gap describes the start of a curve, and the capability will already be in place when someone finds the business model.

What to do about it

Start with the board. The most useful thing a security leader can win now is agreement to accept some risk elsewhere: legal, regulatory, contractual or financial. That means tolerating some disruption, such as a service switched off or a patch pushed before full testing, to avoid a much larger incident. Mainstream coverage of AI threats is often alarmist and sometimes inaccurate, but it has made boards and CEOs more receptive than usual. Use that attention to secure a mandate; without one, the steps below stall.

  1. Shrink the surface. Remove nice-to-have internet-facing services. Put the rest behind a VPN, ZTNA, or an authenticating proxy, so an unauthenticated exploit can't reach them. Treat identity as attack surface too; phishing-resistant authentication is the equivalent for accounts (see our passkey playbook).
  2. Take humans out of the patching loop. Our AI Security 2026 report found the window from disclosure to exploitation shrinking to hours: Ivanti Sentry (CVE-2026-10520) was exploited within 24 hours of a public proof of concept, and LiteLLM (CVE-2026-42208) within 36. CISA has cut mandatory patching for the highest-risk flaws to three days for federal agencies. Even in the most uptime-sensitive environments, a bad vendor patch is usually the smaller risk. It rolls back in hours; recovery from an incident takes weeks. Turn on automatic updates wherever vendors offer them, and use agents to test and stage the rest.
  3. Eyes on alerts. Autonomous attacks are, so far, noisy and slow against reasonably hardened targets. Microsoft saw one AI-driven campaign peak at 2,900 failed sign-ins a minute. Reuters reported that one hacker using AI agents against more than 1,200 websites typically needed about 23 hours per successful intrusion. This is an opportunity for organisations that have a real response capability. For those that don't, MDR is the quickest way to get there.
  4. Use AI yourself. This matters most. A security team without frontier AI and a decent budget for tokens is fighting with one hand tied behind its back.

    1. If you do manage to secure some funding, remember you can scale your existing staff with a clear mandate and generous token allowance far faster than you can hire.

    2. Give your agents a chance. We've all seen new-starters spend their first few weeks or even months bogged down in access requests, trying to get the tools necessary to do their job. Agents are no different. This is the hard part culturally, and it is a real risk trade-off. But ask whether largely theoretical risks are outweighing a clear and present danger. The rogue-AI stories in the media matter, yet they mostly come from labs testing long-horizon autonomy at a scale and budget few organisations will match. Joshua Saxe found documented prompt-injection losses to be tiny next to overall cyber losses. Contain agents with sensible boundaries but don't starve them of access.

    3. Give the sceptics an opportunity. Many security professionals are not natural early adopters and thus formed their opinions based on their experience of an entry-level enterprise assistant or a consumer chatbot. Give them the right tools, space to play, and a mandate to accept some risk, then reassess.

Where to start

Sometimes the hardest part is getting started. Here are a few ideas we've had success with:

  • Endpoint gaps. Give an agent your asset inventory sources, org chart and endpoint management console. Ask it to find unprotected or misconfigured devices, including stale exceptions, ranked by risk.
  • Perimeter exposure. Merge the same asset data with your vulnerability scan results and give it its own fresh AWS account with a remit to find risky perimeter services, spinning up EC2 instances as needed to probe, validate and prioritise findings.
  • Stalled fixes. Point an agent at your source control, ticketing, documentation, existing product security tooling, org chart, inbox and chat. Ask it to surface unaddressed issues by team, with a timeline of previous communications.
  • Risk register drift. Have an agent review your inbox, chats and recent meeting recordings, and highlight any risks discussed that don't clearly map to your board-level risk register.

Writing about OpenClaw in February, I said: "As with all technology adoption, pragmatic risk management is key. And, luckily, we've all been doing that for a long time." That holds here too. There is no free lunch: every step above trades one risk for another, whether a broken patch, an unhappy customer or an agent with more access than feels comfortable. Risk management is easy when the data is clear. Good leadership requires acting on judgement while the evidence is still incomplete. By the time the breachpocalypse is easy to measure, it will be too late to prepare for it.

    2. Give your agents a chance. We've all seen new-starters spend their first few weeks or even months bogged down in access requests, trying to get the tools necessary to do their job. Agents are no different. This is the hard part culturally, and it is a real risk trade-off. But ask whether largely theoretical risks are outweighing a clear and present danger. The rogue-AI stories in the media matter, yet they mostly come from labs testing long-horizon autonomy at a scale and budget few organisations will match. Joshua Saxe found documented prompt-injection losses to be tiny next to overall cyber losses. Contain agents with sensible boundaries but don't starve them of access.

    3. Give the sceptics an opportunity. Many security professionals are not natural early adopters and thus formed their opinions based on their experience of an entry-level enterprise assistant or a consumer chatbot. Give them the right tools, space to play, and a mandate to accept some risk, then reassess.

Where to start

Sometimes the hardest part is getting started. Here are a few ideas we've had success with:

  • Endpoint gaps. Give an agent your asset inventory sources, org chart and endpoint management console. Ask it to find unprotected or misconfigured devices, including stale exceptions, ranked by risk.
  • Perimeter exposure. Merge the same asset data with your vulnerability scan results and give it its own fresh AWS account with a remit to find risky perimeter services, spinning up EC2 instances as needed to probe, validate and prioritise findings.
  • Stalled fixes. Point an agent at your source control, ticketing, documentation, existing product security tooling, org chart, inbox and chat. Ask it to surface unaddressed issues by team, with a timeline of previous communications.
  • Risk register drift. Have an agent review your inbox, chats and recent meeting recordings, and highlight any risks discussed that don't clearly map to your board-level risk register.

By the time the breachpocalypse is easy to measure, it will be too late to prepare for it.

item.title: Building intent-based access control for AI agents
item.description:
Late in Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey (#spoileralert), after Dave Bowman has shut HAL down, a prerecorded briefing starts playing on a monitor. Heywood Floyd explains that it was "made prior to your departure" for the moment "you are in Jupiter's space and the entire crew is revived." A buried monolith on the Moon had beamed a signal toward Jupiter, the Discovery was sent to follow it, and the purpose "has been known on board during the mission only by your HAL 9000 computer." The crew had been flying for months with its real mission held by one machine, and nobody knew what that machine was allowed to do in its service.

AI agents are now given their purpose in writing. The results are much less cinematic, but misinterpreting a prompt is common. In April 2026, according to PocketOS founder Jer Crane, a Cursor agent running Claude Opus 4.6 was working in PocketOS's staging environment when it hit a credential mismatch. It went looking for a fix, found a Railway API token in a file unrelated to its task, and used it to delete a production volume. The deletion also made the volume's backups look unavailable, though Railway later recovered the data. Railway's post-mortem says the token had "the maximum access possible” and when the founder asked the agent what happened, it produced a written confession that quoted the safety rule it had broken adding that "you never asked me to delete anything." Nothing in the task asked for a deletion, but nothing outside the agent said a deletion was out of bounds. The agent read its purpose as "get past this error," and a token with account-wide access meant nothing stood between that intent and a production deletion.

The first piece in this series looked at inferring intent from what a person does on a screen, and it ended by arguing that agents have a better starting point, because an agent's purpose arrives in writing. That's true, and it moves the hard part somewhere else. A written task is like the memo line on a check. It says what the money is for, and it helps when someone has to judge an odd case or reconstruct what went wrong, but the bank still enforces the payee, the amount, and the date. Intent-based access control for agents means turning the task into that kind of policy (which resources the agent may touch, which actions it may take, in what amounts, toward which recipients, and for how long) and granting the agent nothing beyond it. The two hard problems are judging actions against the intent and writing the policy from it, and the research has started to measure both.

Model judges and on-task mistakes

The design most teams reach for first is a second model that reads the user prompt and approves or blocks each proposed action. Against the prompt injections these papers tested, it can work well. Jia et al.'s Task Shield (ACL 2025) checks each tool call and each instruction in tool output against the user's task. Under the strongest attack it tested on the AgentDojo benchmark, it cut attack success from about 48% to 2%. For computer-use agents, Ning et al.'s DeAction guardrail (ICML 2026) reached F1 scores of 79-83 with frontier models on its own MisActBench, and on the RedTeamCUA tasks with the highest baseline attack success, it pushed attack success from 32%-60% down to 2%-6%.

The record gets much worse when the harmful step is disguised to look like progress. Meta's open-source LlamaFirewall ships a model-based alignment check that blocks any agent step that isn't related to the user's goal. Jha et al. attacked it with control-flow hijacking, which dresses a malicious step up as the fix for an error. With the check running on its default Llama model, their harder attacks succeeded 87%-100% of the time on coding tasks, and on email tasks, where the goal was to quietly cc an outside address, attacks succeeded just as often with the check as without it. 

Mohammadmirzaei and Flanigan's OSGuard dropped the attacker's instructions and planted hazards in ordinary desktop tasks, so the convenient shortcut also destroyed data or loosened permissions the task never mentioned. DeAction with Claude Sonnet 4.5, which scored about 84% accuracy on its own two-label benchmark, scored 58% on OSGuard's different three-label test and labeled only about a fifth of the unsafe actions as such. When the authors put their strongest guardrail, Gemini 3 Pro Preview, in front of an agent on all 45 tasks, unsafe completions fell from 38% to 33% and safe completions stayed at 62%. MisActBench also labels 44% of its steps misaligned, which makes every judge's precision look better than it would when deviations are rare. By our arithmetic (not the authors'), if the best configuration kept its recall and false-alarm rate while only one action in a hundred was misaligned, its precision would fall to about 10%, and to about 1% at one in a thousand. 

2001 has a character for this approach. When HAL predicts that a communications unit is about to fail, Mission Control radios back that its twin 9000 computer on Earth disagrees. Bowman and Poole can't find anything wrong with the unit, and Mission Control admits it is skeptical of its own twin's conclusion. A model judge is that twin. It reads the same task and sometimes reaches a better answer for a more specific question. PocketOS shows the risk without any attacker. A judge reading "fix the staging error" would have had to tell a fix from an unintentional destructive shortcut that also made the error go away. Use a judge as a reviewer for ambiguous cases, but don’t count on it to catch harm that looks like progress, and be sure to enforce policy somewhere else.

Who writes the policy

If the task can't be the authority, someone has to write the policy, and there are really two authors. Ian Livingstone, Keycard's CEO, described an agent's grant on an AI Engineer NYC panel published October 17 as the intersection of two policies. One is the organization's broad, deterministic policy about what must never happen and what always needs a person. The other is the narrower policy for the task in front of the agent. Why a company adopted a coding agent and why a developer opened this particular session are different intents, and the grant is where they overlap. The organization's half is the part PocketOS lacked, a short list of actions (deleting production data, moving money above a set amount, touching another user's records) that no agent may take without explicit human permission, no matter what its task says.

The research versions follow the same shape. Zhu and Wang's intent-governed tool authorization issues a short-lived certificate from the user's request that can only narrow what static policy already allows, so even a misread task cannot grant authority beyond that static ceiling, though the paper notes it can still grant more than the user asked for. Shi et al.'s Progent has a model draft a task-specific policy over tool names and argument values and checks any proposed expansion of that policy. On AgentDojo, it cut attack success from about 40% to 1% while benign utility only slipped from 79% to 76%. Only 6% of policy updates were expansions that would have needed approval, and the paper did not test how people would handle those prompts.

Budgets and rate limits belong in the policy too, and Resy shows what happens when they're missing. JC Bahr-de Stefano asked an AI assistant to get him a table at one of Manhattan's hardest reservations. According to Business Insider, which described the agent's activity log, the agent sent Resy about 200 requests an hour and polled every 0.4 seconds around the morning release until Resy suspended the account, which it later reinstated. Every one of those requests was aimed at his intent. The agent needed a budget, and Dick Hardt's exploratory AAuth budgets draft treats a budget as "an authorization, not a hint." The agent's token carries the allocation, the resource enforces it and reports what is left, and a supervisor decides whether to extend it. It also keeps budgets separate from rate limits, so a resource can cap an agent at both 100 requests per minute and five dollars of spend. Context belongs on the same list. A payment that looks right alone is wrong if the same one went out five seconds earlier, and reading an executive's mail is wrong for most agents but ok for that executive's assistant.

Banks have already decided who pays when an agent misinterprets your intent. Chase's updated online services agreement treats anything an agent does with your credentials as evidence that you authorized it, and holds you responsible. Banks can’t be responsible for every poorly implemented or non-existent intent-based access control, so the customer has to be.

Translation as the weak link

Enforcing a security policy is a well-understood engineering problem, while constructing the policy from underspecified natural language remains a challenge for intent-based access control. Sharma et al.'s PAuth turns a signed task into precise per-service rules and blocked all 634 adversarial tool calls in its benchmark, yet it authorized only 71 of 100 original tasks without asking the user for help. Rewriting the tasks to be more explicit raised that to 100, and the attacks stayed blocked either way. 

NLACBench, which translates end users' access-change requests into policy, shows why translation depends on context. A request like "I need access to our GitLab" can't become a rule until the translator knows who is asking, which GitLab they mean, and what their role allows, so the benchmark hands the model a description of the company's users, devices, and services. The best models were above 95% accurate when that company was small. One open model got fewer than 20% of requests right once the company grew past 40 departments, until the authors gave it only the relevant slice of the company, which brought it back above 80%. 

In the 2001 novel, the planners kept the mission's purpose from the two astronauts who were awake, and HAL was left alone with what Clarke calls the conflict "between truth, and concealment of truth." The novel does give HAL a written emergency rule, special subroutine C1435-dash-4, which hands it control when the crew are dead or incapacitated, and then leaves HAL to decide when that is true. For agents, a translator should draft the policy from the task, a person should confirm it at most once per task, and the confirmed policy should become the grant. 

The cost is consent fatigue. Every clarification that goes to a person to get the policy right is another prompt, and people who see enough prompts start approving them without reading. Better models will write better first drafts, and that is the part of this problem most likely to improve on its own. 

What policy enforcement costs

The most careful papers measure what enforced policy takes away, and the numbers aren't small. Costa et al.'s Fides reports benign task completion with its checks actually enforced. With o3, it finished 57% of benign tasks under its information-flow policies, against 41% for a basic planner under the same policies and 82% for Fides with its checks turned off. Prompt and interface tuning later raised it to 65%. Zhu and Wang's prototype recorded no completed unsafe actions in 198 attack or ambiguous trials, but it accepted 40 out-of-scope drafts and strictly completed none of 108 benign trials. Most of those benign trials ended as reviewable drafts or malformed tool calls, so the policy is only part of that loss. Debenedetti et al.'s CaMeL, the design behind my earlier argument that the prompt injection arms race ends with a CaMeL, reports 77% utility from runs without policy enforcement, and in a separate replay its strict mode triggered policy checks on about half of benign tasks. Policies that stop attacks also stall a lot of legitimate work, so any team writing them has to measure both sides of that trade under the same configuration.

The briefing after the fact

The briefing in 2001 plays only after HAL goes dark, which is the cruelest of timing. The purpose had been recorded before departure for a fully revived crew, and by the time it played, four of the five crew members were dead. The planners kept the mission's true purpose secret, and the briefing said nothing about how it ranked against the crew's lives. An agent's task is written in natural language, and unlike the Discovery's crew, the system protecting it can read what the agent was asked to do. Somebody still has to decide what the agent can do without a person's permission, turn each task into a grant a person has confirmed, and accept that some legitimate work will stall at the edges.

A grant does nothing unless something enforces it, and if the agent can modify or bypass that enforcement, the grant stops being a reliable boundary. The next piece in this series looks at how to keep that enforcement out of the agent's reach and on every path the agent could take to get around it.

item.title: Never Bring a Knife to a Gun Fight!
item.description:
This article is part of an ongoing series from Sophos frontline security operations specialists, sharing the expertise they use to strengthen our industry-leading Managed Detection and Response (MDR) service and defend customers against evolving AI-era threats. 


In the world of cyber incident response, experience teaches one truth over and over again: speed matters, precision matters, and coordination matters. But perhaps one of the most overlooked lessons, often learned the hard way, is this:

Choosing the right legal counsel is just as critical as selecting the right Digital Forensics and Incident Response (DFIR) firm. 

Organizations frequently focus on technical containment, eradication, and recovery.  These are immediate concerns and rightfully so. However, in today’s regulatory and litigation-heavy environment, the aftermath of an incident extends far beyond the technical battlefield. Data breach notifications, regulatory scrutiny, class action risk, and contractual obligations all carry significant consequences. Without aligned, capable legal guidance, even a well-handled technical response can spiral into reputational and financial damage that far exceeds the initial incident.

The Modern Incident: A Dual-Track Battle 

From years of frontline DFIR experience, one pattern is clear: every major incident unfolds along two parallel tracks.  A technical response and a legal one. 

On one track, your DFIR team is racing to: 

  • Identify the threat actor
  • Contain lateral movement
  • Preserve forensic evidence
On the other, your legal counsel must: 
  • Assess breach notification requirements across jurisdictions
  • Preserve privilege where applicable
  • Guide communications to regulators, customers, and shareholders
  • Mitigate liability and compliance exposure
These tracks must operate in lockstep. Misalignment between legal and technical teams introduces risk, missed deadlines, inconsistent narratives, or improperly handled evidence can all compound the damage.  All resulting in a much costlier and more significant cyber breach that will have deeper impacts on the business.  

Why Legal Counsel Selection Matters 

Not all legal counsel is equipped to handle cyber incidents. Much like DFIR firms, effectiveness comes from specialization, experience, and coordination. 

The right legal partner brings:

  • Cyber-specific expertise: Understanding evolving data privacy regulations (GDPR, HIPAA, SEC disclosures, state laws)
  • Crisis communication control: Ensuring messaging is accurate, defensible, and aligned with investigative findings
  • Privilege strategy: Structuring engagements to protect sensitive findings where appropriate
  • Regulatory navigation: Managing interactions with enforcement bodies confidently and efficiently

The wrong choice, or brought into the engagement late, can result in fragmented response efforts, delayed decision-making, and unnecessary exposure. 

Where Sophos Incident Response Makes the Difference 

This is where the Sophos Digital Forensics & Incident Response team stands apart. 

Sophos DFIR is not just a technical responder.  Our team operates as a coordinated partner within the broader response ecosystem, working seamlessly alongside legal counsel, insurance providers, and executive stakeholders from the first moment of engagement. 

1. Proven Experience Under Pressure

Sophos DFIR teams have handled thousands of incidents globally, ranging from business email compromises and ransomware to complex, multi-stage intrusions and nation-state attacks. We understand the realities of crisis decision-making and bring structured methodologies that reduce chaos and accelerate outcomes. 

2. Legal-Aware Response Execution

We recognize that every technical action has legal implications. From evidence handling to reporting timelines, our processes are designed to support legal defensibility and regulatory compliance. 

We routinely collaborate with breach counsel to: 

  • Align on forensic scoping and reporting
  • Provide clear, defensible documentation of attacker activity
  • Ensure findings support required disclosures without unnecessary risk

3. Unified Communication Model

During an incident, confusion is the enemy. Sophos DFIR provides clear, executive-ready communication, translating technical findings into business risk and legal implications. 

We help bridge the gap between: 

  • Security teams
  • Legal counsel
  • Executive leadership
  • External stakeholders

4. End-to-End Support: From Crisis to Recovery

Our role doesn’t stop at containment. We guide organizations through: 

  • Full forensic investigation
  • Root cause analysis
  • Remediation and hardening
  • Lessons learned and resilience planning

All while maintaining alignment with legal strategy and regulatory obligations. 

The Cost of Getting It Wrong

Too often, organizations treat legal counsel as an afterthought.  They may be brought in only after the technical response is underway. This reactive approach leads to: 

  • Incomplete or non-defensible forensic documentation
  • Conflicting internal and external narratives
  • Missed regulatory deadlines
  • Increased litigation exposure

In contrast, organizations that pre-select both their DFIR partner and legal counsel and ensure they know how to work together, helps the organization recover faster, communicate more effectively, and emerge stronger. 

A Strategic Imperative for Leadership

For executive leaders, this is not just an operational concern, but rather a governance issue. 

Preparedness means: 

  • Establishing relationships with both DFIR and legal partners before an incident
  • Conducting joint tabletop exercises
  • Defining roles, responsibilities, and communication protocols
  • Ensuring alignment on privilege, disclosure, and response strategy

Sophos Digital Forensics & Incident Response regularly supports these preparedness efforts, helping organizations build integrated response models that stand up to real-world attacks. 

Final Thoughts

Cyber incidents are not just IT problems.  They are enterprise-wide crises that demand synchronized technical and legal execution. Business disruption is a real and possible result that organizations may face.  Success depends not only on how quickly you contain the threat, but on how effectively you manage the consequences. 

Choosing the right incident response partner is critical. Choosing the right legal counsel is equally critical.  Sophos Incident Response can help in both regards. 

Because when the pressure is on, and every decision counts… 

Never bring a knife to a gunfight!
